title: Optical Ion Clock with Engineered Immunity to Motion-Induced Frequency Shifts
authors: Mark Lide, Wesley Hardin, Christian Sanner
abstract: Spectroscopic frequency shifts due to residual motion of the probed atoms significantly contribute to the uncertainty budgets of state-of-the-art optical ion clocks. For clock transitions with second-order Doppler and quadratic Stark shifts of opposite signs, it is possible to configure electrodynamic ion confinement such that these two shift effects become anticorrelated causing zero net shift. Here, we introduce a spectroscopic interrogation protocol which leads, for systems with unknown and varying motional energy gain rates, to first-order auto-suppression of corresponding frequency shifts without requiring the opposite-sign configuration. We experimentally demonstrate the proposed method on a new ytterbium ion optical clock probing the 467 nm electric octupole (E3) transition, where the combined fractional uncertainty contribution from motion-induced frequency shifts is reduced from $1.3\times10^{-18}$ to $0.3\times10^{-18}$. An interleaved optical frequency ratio measurement against ytterbium's electric quadrupole transition (E2) at 435 nm delivers an E3/E2 frequency ratio of $0.932 \,829 \,404 \,530 \,965 \, 340 (39)$. Combined with previously published ratio data this leads to a limit for a potential fractional temporal variation of the fine-structure constant of $2.4 (2.7) \times 10^{-19}/$yr, in agreement with existing bounds.
summary: This paper details a novel spectroscopic interrogation protocol designed to suppress systematic frequency shifts caused by residual atomic motion in optical ion clocks. By engineering the interrogation sequence, the authors achieved a substantial reduction in the motion-induced uncertainty budget for a $	ext{Yb}^+$ clock. This improved precision allows for setting tighter limits on fundamental physical constants like the fine-structure constant.
main_problem: Residual motion-induced frequency shifts significantly limit the uncertainty budgets of state-of-the-art optical ion clocks.
main_result: The authors experimentally reduced the motion-induced systematic uncertainty contribution from $1.3	imes10^{-18}$ to $0.3	imes10^{-18}$ using a novel interrogation protocol.
method: They introduced a spectroscopic interrogation protocol, based on a Ramsey-style sequence with detuned pulses, to achieve first-order auto-suppression of motion-induced shifts.
model_or_system: The experiment uses a single laser-cooled ytterbium ion ($	ext{Yb}^+$) confined in an endcap radio-frequency Paul trap, probing the 467 nm electric octupole (E3) transition.
key_observables:
The primary observables are the residual clock frequency shift ($\Delta
u_{	ext{ENGS}}$) and the measured E3/E2 frequency ratio.
important_parameters: The uncertainty reduction factor is key, moving from $1.3	imes10^{-18}$ to $0.3	imes10^{-18}$, and the resulting limit on the fine-structure constant variation is $2.4(2.7) 	imes 10^{-19}/$yr.
main_assumptions: The auto-cancellation scheme only provides first-order cancellation and does not correct for imperfect micromotion compensation.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of motion-induced shifts, then details the theoretical basis for the auto-suppression protocol using pulse engineering, presents the experimental implementation on $	ext{Yb}^+$, and concludes with the measured uncertainty reduction and fundamental constant limits.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant advancement in precision measurement techniques for quantum systems, directly addressing systematic noise sources (motion) in trapped-ion clocks using advanced quantum control sequences.
